display_title: Interesting results for adversarial evaluation but weak for interpretability

content.title: Interesting results for adversarial evaluation but weak for interpretability
content.review:
This paper investigates approaches for multimodal machine translation (MMT) and their adversarial evaluation. The contributions are mainly twofold: (a) a conventional and a retrieval-based MMT systems which marginally improve over existing methods, and (b) an analysis of gains given by two regularization approaches in text-only MT and two MMT systems, showing that these techniques achieve similar gains to the visual modality.

---

Strong points:
1) An interesting study that highlights how text-only baselines can perform similarly to MMT systems. I think this result is the main contribution of this paper
2) Rigorous experimental setup, leading to a controlled study of several MMT systems
3) It is interesting to see confirmed that tiny transformers perform better in Multi30k (including multimodal ones)

---

Weak points:
1) Misleading title: From the title, I expected a thorough analysis of several MMT systems, while findings are basically based on the proposed systems
2) Forced interpretability direction: I find that interpretability is a major point in the motivation of this work, however, this only corresponds to a gate vector in the Gated Fusion model. As also written in the paper, similar gates have been used in the literature. In addition, the gate used in this paper -- used to weight the image representation -- is a function of both image and text representations, and not of the image only
3) The end of paragraph 1 in page 2 claims that images lead to smaller network weights but I do not see this claim supported in the experiments
3) The paper also claims SOTA performance of the new models, while (a) they achieve minimal gains in most of the test sets, and (b) the results in Fig 1 make this claim even harder to believe. I find the results in Section 5.2 really informative, and, as the aim of the paper is not SOTA, I think this should be toned down
4) Section 5.1 hints at multiple MMT systems but interpretability results (Table 2) are only given for the Gated Fusion model

---

Minor points:
1) How is statistical significance evaluated in Table 1?
2) Given the (nice!) small size of most models, I would really be interested in seeing the variance of these models when trained multiple times
3) It would be great for reproducibility if you released code for the models and experiments

---

To sum up, I think that this paper contains interesting results (especially about adversarial evaluation) but I don't personally find the general interpretability of MMT systems motivation strongly backed up by the current results.

---
Post rebuttal:
Thank you for the thorough responses. I still believe that presentation should be improved to effectively convey the findings in this paper. Nevertheless, the results are interesting for the community (although I would deeper analyses for claiming interpretability).

content.title: More results and analysis
content.comment:
> Q1: Misleading title: From the title, I expected a thorough analysis of several MMT systems, while findings are basically based on the proposed systems

A1: Although we focus more on analyzing the proposed models, we also evaluate the performance of a series of popular MMT systems under a small model size. Compared to the original model performance in their papers, we find that many MMT systems are suffering from overfitting due to the large model size. Additionally, our proposed systems, which outperform existing models, witness similar gains and demonstrate the source of those gains explicitly.


> Q2: Forced interpretability direction: I find that interpretability is a major point in the motivation of this work, however, this only corresponds to a gate vector in the Gated Fusion model. As also written in the paper, similar gates have been used in the literature. In addition, the gate used in this paper -- used to weight the image representation -- is a function of both image and text representations, and not of the image only

A2: Thanks for the suggestion, learning the gate only condition on image is another design alternative that worth investigating. 
Apart from Gated Fusion, the retrieval-based model (RMMT) also has a interpretable module. Under the proposed joint training objective, we reward the retriever when the images retrieved can improve translation. This lets the model decide by itself the usefulness of visual information. If the model learns to perform meaningful retrieval(retrieved images are semantically relevant to sentences), then we can conclude that images can help translation or our MMT model indeed exploits visual information. We can further use tools like attention heatmap to analyze how the model perceives those images.  However, as we discussed in Sec5.2, we observe that the retriever collapsed and always retrieve the same images regardless of input sentences. The interpretation is that the model does not find utilizing images in translation helpful, at least in our experiments. 

> Q3: The paper also claims SOTA performance of the new models, while (a) they achieve minimal gains in most of the test sets, and (b) the results in Fig 1 make this claim even harder to believe. I find the results in Section 5.2 really informative, and, as the aim of the paper is not SOTA, I think this should be toned down. 

A3: We agree with the reviewer that although our models achieve good performance, the gains are still marginal. The focus of this paper is more on analyzing how visual features affect MMT systems. We try to answer the question where the gains in MMT systems indeed come from. 

Minor points:

> Q4: How is statistical significance evaluated in Table 1?

A4: We follow Koehn, 2004 (Statistical significance tests for machine translation evaluation ) to perform the significance test. https://github.com/pytorch/translate/blob/master/pytorch_translate/bleu_significance.py

> Q5: Given the (nice!) small size of most models, I would really be interested in seeing the variance of these models when trained multiple times

A5: Due to time constraints we only tried on Transformer-Tiny and Gated Fusion-Tiny. We run with 3 different random seeds and report the Standard Deviation. We find that the models are quite robust to randomness, Transformer(+- 0.17) Gated Fusion(+-0.2)

> Q6: It would be great for reproducibility if you released code for the models and experiments

A6: Sure, we plan to release the code after the anonymity period.

content.title: This paper is well motivated and well written. The method is simple yet effective. The analysis is insufficient to support the claim.
content.review:
This work revisits the recent development of neural multimodal machine translation. The authors split the current MMT models into two categories, among which both conventional MMT and retrieval-based MMT models are evaluated. Experimental results on Multi30K show that the small models achieve SOTA. According to the observation, the MMT models tend to ignore the multimodal information, and the analysis indicates that the benefits from multimodal models might result from some regularization effects. The hypothesis is further verified by adding random noise and using large weight decay.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Strengths:

1. This work investigates MMT from an interpretable perspective. This study is well motivated and the paper is well written. 

2. The method for the MMT task is simple yet effective, especially the small model shows competitive results on the Multi30K dataset, which overcomes the over-fitting problems in previous larger models.

3. Detailed analysis of the experimental results highlights the effectiveness of regularization on the Multi30K dataset. 

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Weaknesses:

1.  A concern is whether the regularization effects stand generally. The conclusion drawn from only one dataset would not be convincing enough, especially for the reason that the Multi30K dataset is quite small, and the sentences are short and repetitive.
Since there is a retrieval-based method in this work, how about the performance on larger scale WMT tasks? The analysis of different lengths of sentences from Multi30K would also be helpful. The analysis is weak to support the claim that the visual features work as regularization. 

2. The overfitting issue on Multi30K was disclosed before. Using images for regularized training was also not new. It is not clear how the findings in this work could help future research. 
    Reference: Caglayan, Ozan, et al. "LIUM-CVC Submissions for WMT17 Multimodal Translation Task." Proceedings of the Second Conference on Machine Translation. 2017.

3. There is no comparison on how the visual information affects different sizes of models, i.e., the base, small, and tiny models in the paper, which would be potential as supportive evidence to analyze whether the visual information could alleviate the overfitting in larger models. Otherwise, there would be a concern that the improvements would come from the less overfitting on the tiny model, i.e., a very competitive baseline. 

4. The two “proposed” models are very similar to the public ones. The gated fusion method is actually used in previous MMT models, as clarified in the paper. The retrieval-based method, including cross-modal image retrieval, was also studied before. A clarification would be beneficial.  Therefore, the statement “proposing two interpretable MMT models” would suffer from overclaiming to some extent. I would suggest to rephrase it as “providing” or “presenting” the two methods instead of “proposing” ones.
    Reference: Zhang, Zhuosheng, et al. "Probing contextualized sentence representations with visual awareness." arXiv preprint arXiv:1911.02971 (2019).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Minor Comments:

Line 7 in the introduction, form -> from?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Overall Recommendation:

This paper is well written and presents good insights. However,  the experiment part is weak and lacks some important comparisons to support the hypothesis.  Also, it is not clear how the findings in this work could help future research. Hopefully, the authors can address my concern in the rebuttal period. 

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Post rebuttal

Thank you for your detailed response.
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

replying_to: Replying to This paper is well motivated and well written. The method is simple yet effective. The analysis is insufficient to support the claim.

content.title: response part 1
content.comment:
> Q1: The conclusion drawn from only one dataset would not be convincing enough, especially for the reason that the Multi30K dataset is quite small, and the sentences are short and repetitive. A concern is whether the regularization effects stand generally. Since there is a retrieval-based method in this work, how about the performance on larger scale WMT tasks? The analysis of different lengths of sentences from Multi30K would also be helpful.
 
A1: Thanks for the suggestion. We now also evaluate on a large-scale video-based dataset (please check Appendix B). For retrieval-based method and NMT tasks, in our first submission, we have evaluated on IWSLT14'En-De(now in Appendix E), which is close to WMT'16 En-Ro in terms of data scale.
We also tried WMT'14 En-De but observed no improvement when introducing visual information. But so far we only have time and computing resources to train the model once, we believe that with the appropriate tuning we might be able to see improvement as in Zhang et al, 2020 and as in our IWSLT14’EN-DE experiments. 
We also analyze how the gating weight \lambda varies from sentences of different lengths. But observe no significant difference between sentences. 
 
 
> Q2: The overfitting issue on Multi30K was disclosed before. Using images for regularized training was also not new. It is not clear how the findings in this work could help future research. Reference: Caglayan, Ozan, et al. "LIUM-CVC Submissions for WMT17 Multimodal Translation Task." Proceedings of the Second Conference on Machine Translation. 2017.
 
A2: We agree with the reviewer that the overfitting issue on Multi30K is not new, however, this is not the main focus or contribution of our paper. Although Caglayan, Ozan, et al. did use l2 regularization in their experiments, they merely used it as a regular training trick to avoid overfitting and did not mention/discuss any relation between the regularization effect and the use of images. In fact, their results suggest that even with l2 reg, the NMT baselines are still significantly outperformed by MMT systems, which is in contrast to our finding that NMT+reg can achieve compatible performance with MMT systems. We hypothesize the reason being that they directly use l2 reg with Adam, resulting in issues like reported in "Fixing weight decay regularization in Adam". 
 
 
> Q3:There is no comparison on how the visual information affects different sizes of models, i.e., the base, small, and tiny models in the paper, which would be potential as supportive evidence to analyze whether the visual information could alleviate the overfitting in larger models. Otherwise, there would be a concern that the improvements would come from the less overfitting on the tiny model, i.e., a very competitive baseline.

A3: Thanks for the suggestion. We add experiments for large models + visual information. Due to time and resources constraints, we only evaluated on the “base” setting, which is widely used in most MMT papers.  The results show that injecting visual information into large models exhibit a similar gain as regularizing the Transformer with weight decay. 
```
				              en-de’16  ’17   ’coco   en-fr’16    ’17   ’coco

Text-only Transformer base	38.33	31.36	27.54	60.60	53.16	42.83	

  +weight decay  0.1          39.92	32.19	29.11    61.93	54.34	43.93

imagination	               39.51	31.52	28.33	61.43	52.84	44.29

Gated Fusion                  38.75	31.90	27.94	61.21	53.67	42.70

RMMT-static	               39.18	30.77	30.38	61.10	53.20	44.01


Those results suggest that visual info can alleviate overfitting in large models as regularization does.

content.title: response part 2
content.comment:
> Q4: The two “proposed” models are very similar to the public ones. The gated fusion method is actually used in previous MMT models, as clarified in the paper. The retrieval-based method, including cross-modal image retrieval, was also studied before. A clarification would be beneficial. Therefore, the statement “proposing two interpretable MMT models” would suffer from overclaiming to some extent. I would suggest to rephrase it as “providing” or “presenting” the two methods instead of “proposing” ones. Reference: Zhang, Zhuosheng, et al. "Probing contextualized sentence representations with visual awareness." arXiv preprint arXiv:1911.02971 (2019).

A4: We agree with the reviewer that the gated fusion method is not new (also clarified in the paper). For the retrieval-based models, our RMMT-static does share some similarity with Zhang et al., 2019, 2020 (we do mention this in Sec4.3 and will discuss more connections between them). But our RMMT model differs in the way that we take advantage of recent findings that joint training of the model with the retriever improves the performance, if the database in the retrieval system offers beneficial information. Different from RMMT, Zhang et al., 2019, 2020’s retrievers are pre-trained and fixed during final training. Besides, as mentioned in the paper as well as pointed out by Reviewer 1 and 4, we are the first to use gating and retrieval-based methods for the purpose of analyzing and interpreting MMT systems, to the best of our knowledge.  
 
> Q5: A lack of some implementation details. How about the vocabulary size? Are the vocab shared for different languages?

A5: We use a shared vocabulary for both En-De (9,712 tokens) and En-Fr (9,544 tokens), as stated in Sec 4.1.
 
> Q6: it is not clear how the findings in this work could help future research.

A6: As pointed out by the reviewer and discussed in the conclusion section, we believe that sophisticated MMT models are necessary for effective grounding of visual context into translation. Their effectiveness might be impaired by limitations in Multi30K, which contains simple, short and repetitive sentences. In the future, if new benchmarks are created, our work can provide a convenient way to investigate whether new datasets require meaningful visual grounding or not, and save time and effort of trial and error.  In summary, although our work can not provide direct suggestions to researchers about how to design better MMT systems, it helps clear some confusion on MMT and stress the importance of the interpretability of MMT systems, calling for a more explicit explanation of the system improvements over the text-only baselines.

display_title: An interesting work yet there is space for improvement.

content.title: An interesting work yet there is space for improvement.
content.review:
Summary:


This paper tries to provide a better understanding of whether visual features are helpful for Multimodal Machine Translation (MMT). It is not new in the literature that visual features are found to be actually not that useful. However, the contribution in this paper is to provide another interesting analysis of this problem. In their work, they propose to use the so called fusion model, which mixtures two embedding spaces of text and images with a weight learned by an attention mechanism. The another interesting contribution of the model is to use the so called retriever component, which is basically an inner product between embedding of text and embedding of image. The goal of the retriever component is to generate more diverse images during training (say top_K), not only the ground truth. These techniques are definitely not new in the literature. These are a combination of different methods proposed before in the literature (for different NLP problems). However, the work claims that this is the first time it was used for the purpose of understanding the contribution of visual features in MMD. And I agree with that, to the best of my knowledge.  Finally, they claim that what visual features do is all about regularization.


On the positive side, this work is nice with interesting findings.  I personally learnt useful things from this work. 

On the other hand, however, I have several concerns regarding the writing/presentation as well as questions regarding experiment results.

1. Writing/presentation: Writing could be improved regarding the contributions of the paper and structure of experiments to validate them. The current version is written in such a way that is not clear what the paper ultimately aims for. If part of it is about that the proposed model that achieves SOTA result, it is definitely not clear where the improvement comes from (e.g. whether it is because of the use of pretrained models including ResNet-50, BERT, and Text-to-Image-Retrieval task, or because of your proposed model itself). If part of it is about analyzing the effects of visual features, while it is interesting, I feel not totally satisfied in the experiment results (see below for the detail reason why). 

Writing could be also improved regarding the presentation. For instance, the work has different baselines but it is not totally clear to me what the baselines are for. Are they simply for reference? Or are they there because the paper tries to show that that the model achieves SOTA results? This make me confused. 

Another different example is the presentation of decoding. “Fast Decoding” algorithm is mentioned quickly without any explanation. I understood this algorithm belongs to other work, but since decoding is very important in your model, it is not satisfied to see it was presented quickly. Finally, I have a difficulty with the section "``What does the retriever learn" because the explanation is not clear to me. If you present a gradient formula from the paper, you should make it easier for readers to know at least why it derives that way. I understood this is proposed by another work and you try to apply it into your model, but at least some explanation might help.

2. Experiment results: First, if visual features are ignored, why does fusion model is better than the balance model? If it is because the fusion model discards visual features, then why does the fusion model is better than the Transformer Tiny? I feel the contribution is very nice but the problem is evident are not clear in the paper. 

Second, if you found regularization help the baseline achieve similar or better visual features, it is not convinced with the conclusion that what visual features do is about regularization. What if they learn different things but somewhat on-par results? I think readers are convinced if the paper provides much more solid argument than what is in the current version.

In summary, the paper is interesting. However, I suggested it should be revised significantly to improve readability as well as make arguments more solid.


Other minor notes:


- The baseline isn’t -> is not

- Following standard practices, we use a pre-trained BERT model2 to obtain the “pooled” representation of the sequence (denoted as BERTCLS(x)). -> I am curious by poor do you remove the 0 token?

- RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED MMT - I understand the formula but at least there is a reference of p_{\theta}(y|x, z)) using the gate fusion MMT.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Improve readability and new experimental results.
content.comment:
> Q1: Writing/presentation: Writing could be improved regarding the contributions of the paper and structure of experiments to validate them. The current version is written in such a way that is not clear what the paper ultimately aims for. If part of it is about that the proposed model that achieves SOTA result, it is definitely not clear where the improvement comes from (e.g. whether it is because of the use of pretrained models including ResNet-50, BERT, and Text-to-Image-Retrieval task, or because of your proposed model itself). If part of it is about analyzing the effects of visual features, while it is interesting, I feel not totally satisfied in the experiment results (see below for the detail reason why).

A1: Thanks for the suggestion, we will revise accordingly. Although we do achieve SOTA results on some testbeds, this is not the focus of our paper. Since we are proposing models to analyze the effects of visual features, it's necessary for our models to be able to exploit visual information effectively in whatever ways first, otherwise, the analysis will be meaningless. Please refer to “response to all reviewers” for more evidence to support our findings. 
And as our findings suggest, the improvement actually comes from some regularization effect, rather than from BERT, ResNet-50, etc, at least on the dataset we evaluated. 

> Q2: Writing could be also improved regarding the presentation. For instance, the work has different baselines but it is not totally clear to me what the baselines are for. Are they simply for reference? Or are they there because the paper tries to show that the model achieves SOTA results? This makes me confused.

A2: Those MMT baselines are selected to set a ground for comparison. Since we are using a very different(much smaller) model size, it would be necessary to evaluate how existing methods perform under this setting and see whether they will still exhibit improvement. Besides, as mentioned above, to demonstrate the effectiveness of our models (by comparing to both NMT and MMT baselines) is the preliminary of meaningful analysis.

> Q3: I have difficulty understand “Fast Decoding” algorithm and the section "What does the retriever learn"

A3: We revised these two sections accordingly to make them more readable.

> Q4: Experiment results: First, if visual features are ignored, why does fusion model is better than the balance model? If it is because the fusion model discards visual features, then why does the fusion model is better than the Transformer Tiny? I feel the contribution is very nice but the problem is evident are not clear in the paper.

A4: Balance Fusion forces the model to fuse text repr with visual repr and average them. This is a very rigid setup, it assumes that source sentence and image contribute equally to the translation, which is not true in most of the cases. Gated fusion, on the other hand, will not suffer from this problem because we let the model decide by itself how much visual information it needs. In the case where images can help disambiguate translation, we would expect the gating value to be larger (use more visual information). While when a source sentence can provide sufficient context for translation, we would expect the gating value to be smaller, thus introducing less redundant information(potential noise). Note that even in the case that the gating value is near zero, it is different from saying that visual features are totally ignored or discarded.

> Q5: Second, if you found regularization help the baseline achieve similar or better visual features, it is not convinced with the conclusion that what visual features do is about regularization. What if they learn different things but somewhat on-par results? I think readers are convinced if the paper provides much more solid argument than what is in the current version.

A5: We add more evidence to support our findings, please refer to “response to all reviewers” for detailed results. 

> Q6: Following standard practices, we use a pre-trained BERT model2 to obtain the “pooled” representation of the sequence (denoted as BERTCLS(x)). -> I am curious by poor do you remove the 0 token?

A6: The "pooled" representation here can be understood as that we use the first([CLS]) token's representation as a sentence representation, as feed it into later network components as input. We did not perform removal in the process.

display_title: Need more theoretical or experimental support for the claims

content.title: Need more theoretical or experimental support for the claims
content.review:
Summary: This paper focuses on studying the contribution of visual information in the context of multimodal machine translation. The paper motivates the utility of explicit approaches for conditioning visual information in the form of two methods a) gated fusion of visual information, and b) an image retrieval module augmenting a standard multimodal machine translation model. In both cases, the model learns to condition visual information when the model deems it necessary for translation. The experiments are conducted on the multimodal machine translation shared task datasets and IWSLT datasets. The paper emphasises the difference in BLEU as an indication of the performance of the systems. The degree to which gating allows for visual information and difference of BLEU between learned and static retrieval-based models are highlighted as indicating the underutilisation of visual information. The paper then hypothesises that conditioning the visual information acts as a regularizer and proceeds to empirically validate using experiments where the models are conditioned with random noise instead of visual information. The paper also tries to contrast and show that the effect of conditioning on visual information for the current multimodal machine translation models is similar to regularisation using weight decay. The paper concludes with this final observation stating that the visual context is beneficial as a regulariser than as previously assumed as ``'informative' set of cues.

Comments: The paper is well written and looks at an interesting problem of visual conditioning and its utility. As the paper suggests, it is generally not clear where and when does visual information help the process of machine translation. The proposal of investigating the visual contribution using a gated approach and a retrieval-based approach (both are not new proposals but are used here for interpretation) is interesting. 

However, there are several problems that I came across when perusing the paper. The paper makes an assumption that the translation of the samples in the dataset will improve with visual information. Perhaps this may be a case for a proportion of samples as is indicated in Barrault et al, 2018.  A similar observation regarding a small proportion of samples that could exploit visual information was reported in Caglayan et al, 2019. The results in both gating and retrieval-based models experiments seem to indicate that it is indeed exploiting visual information over a fraction of examples. 

While using BLEU to compare systems is usually sufficient, in the context of this paper, however, I wonder if better qualitative analyses of the translated samples would help uncover the contributions of images. 

The training dynamics in the proposed models is also unclear. It would also be worthwhile looking deeply into the training dynamics --- understanding how visual information is exploited during training. The only observations that the paper seems to make are by looking at performance over various testsplits. 

The experiments with random noise and weight decay show that the models seem to have better aggregate BLEU scores. While this is interesting and likely has some correlation with experiments where the conditioning is done with images, I don’t think this is sufficient to claim that the visual information is acting as a regularizer. I think going deeper into qualitative evaluation would be helpful. Perhaps BLEU as a metric is unable to elicit the difference. At this moment, it lacks both theoretical and experimental support. 

Minor concerns: 

a) Regarding “to ensure fair comparison and minimize training/environmental differences, all the above baselines are implemented by ourselves based on FairSeq and with the same set of hyper-parameters”. I wonder if experimenting with same set of hyper-parameters is a good idea as some of these are also involve platform changes.  Perchance the hyperparameters are suboptimal in the new implementation with PyTorch backend? 

b) As the experiments are conducted with adam optimiser, I wonder if the weight-decay experiments might have similar artefacts as demonstrated in Loshchilov et al, 2019. 

c) The experiments with IWSLT dataset in the Appendix is unclear. It is very difficult to comprehend the setup. What was the set of images here? 


Decision: Rated 4 

References: 
Barrault, Loïc, et al. "Findings of the third shared task on multimodal machine translation." 2018.

Caglayan, Ozan, et al. "Probing the need for visual context in multimodal machine translation." 2019.

Loshchilov, Ilya, and Frank Hutter. "Fixing weight decay regularization in Adam." 2019
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

content.title: response part 1
content.comment:
> Q1: However, there are several problems that I came across when perusing the paper. The paper makes an assumption that the translation of the samples in the dataset will improve with visual information. Perhaps this may be a case for a proportion of samples as is indicated in Barrault et al, 2018. A similar observation regarding a small proportion of samples that could exploit visual information was reported in Caglayan et al, 2019. The results in both gating and retrieval-based models experiments seem to indicate that it is indeed exploiting visual information over a fraction of examples.
 
A1: We will revise the framing to avoid confusion. Both Barrault et al, 2018 and Caglayan et al, 2019 are suggesting that the images were perceived as “needed” in the translation because images can help disambiguate words or better understand the source description.
Although our gating and retrieval-based models achieved certain improvement, we find that they exploit visual information in a way that differs from those previously conceived (like the ones  above and Julia Ive et al, 2019). In particular, in our visual awareness experiments, we find that about 70% of gating values are zero (i.e correlate with previous works that most samples do not exploit visual information). Even for those samples that indeed exploit visual features, our further experiments find that visual features function in a way similar to regularization methods in practice. 
Distilling Translations with Visual Awareness. Julia Ive1, Pranava Madhyastha and Lucia Specia 2019.
 

> Q2: While using BLEU to compare systems is usually sufficient, in the context of this paper, however, I wonder if better qualitative analyses of the translated samples would help uncover the contributions of images.

A2: Thanks for pointing this out. Besides BLEU, we now also add results on METEOR(a more advanced metric that correlates better with human judgement). We find that results based on Meteor are mostly consistent with those based on BLEU. Please refer to Appendix D for detailed results.
 

> Q3: The training dynamics in the proposed models is also unclear. It would also be worthwhile looking deeply into the training dynamics --- understanding how visual information is exploited during training. The only observations that the paper seems to make are by looking at performance over various testsplits.

A3: Thanks for the suggestion. By analyzing how the Gated Fusion model weights images over time, we find evidence that the model indeed learns to translate without utilizing rich visual cues from the images.  Please refer to Appendix C for a detailed response.
 

> Q4: The experiments with random noise and weight decay show that the models seem to have better aggregate BLEU scores. While this is interesting and likely has some correlation with experiments where the conditioning is done with images, I don’t think this is sufficient to claim that the visual information is acting as a regularizer. I think going deeper into qualitative evaluation would be helpful. Perhaps BLEU as a metric is unable to elicit the difference. At this moment, it lacks both theoretical and experimental support.

A4: We now include the METEOR metric in our evaluation. METEOR consistently demonstrates higher correlation with human judgments than BLEU does in independent evaluations such as EMNLP WMT 2011 and NIST Metrics MATR 2010. (https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~alavie/METEOR/) We also provide new evidence(new experiments and evaluation on new dataset) to support our findings. Please refer to "response to all reviewers" for a detailed response.

content.title: response part 2
content.comment:
Minor concerns:

> Q5: Regarding “to ensure fair comparison and minimize training/environmental differences, all the above baselines are implemented by ourselves based on FairSeq and with the same set of hyper-parameters”. I wonder if experimenting with the same set of hyper-parameters is a good idea as some of these are also involve platform changes. Perchance the hyperparameters are suboptimal in the new implementation with PyTorch backend?

A5: By the same set of hyper-parameters, we mean the set of parameters we found through grid search that works well across multiple baselines and our methods, not the set of parameters from the original paper. We do so to 1) control experimental variables 2) reduce computing cost since we don’t have to perform grid search for each system.
 Although performing extensive parameter search individually can find the best parameters for each system, and maybe further improve some of them’s performance, we find the improvement quite marginal and do not affect our conclusion.
 
> Q6: As the experiments are conducted with adam optimizer, I wonder if the weight-decay experiments might have similar artefacts as demonstrated in Loshchilov et al, 2019.

A6: Our implementation is based on FairSeq, which has fixed this issue, as pointed out in https://github.com/pytorch/fairseq/blob/master/fairseq/optim/adam.py L100.
 
> Q7: The experiments with IWSLT dataset in the Appendix is unclear. It is very difficult to comprehend the setup. What was the set of images here?

A7: For IWSLT, we follow the setup from Zhang et al., 2020 and use the same set of images as those Multi30K experiments (since there is no image corpus associated with IWSLT). So basically, for each sentence from IWSLT, we retrieve an image from Multi30k image base, and use the retrieved images to help translation.
Neural machine translation with universal visual representation. Zhuosheng Zhang et al, 2020

replying_to: Replying to Good for Misconceived Reasons: Revisiting Neural Multimodal Machine Translation

content.title: Response to all reviewers
content.comment:
Dear reviewers,
 
Thanks for your constructive feedback and patience. The major concern shared by most of the reviewers is that the experimental results so far can not strongly support our findings. Thus we provide some new evidence here to further substantiate our claim. 
 
In an overview, we present:
 
(1) New metric. Results based on Meteor rather than just BLEU. (Appendix D)
(2) Running time analysis of the proposed models, in particular, how they exploit images over time. (Appendix C)
(3) Experimental results on a new dataset: VaTex, a video-based MMT corpus. (Appendix B)
 
We summarize our key findings below. Please refer to the revised paper for more detail.
 
(1) Evaluation based on Meteor demonstrates similar trends as those based on BLEU.
 
(2) Take Gated Fusion for example. We find that at the beginning of training, the model relies heavily on image information (i.e. assigns high gating weights to images). As the training continues, the weights gradually decrease to near zero. In plain words, the model learns to translate without utilizing rich visual cues from the images. 
 
(3) Our evaluation results on the video-based MMT task (VaTex) are mostly consistent with those on Multi30K, which further validate our findings. 
 
 Due to time constraints, some experiments or some baseline systems are missing from those new results. Such as random noise experiments on VaTex, which are very time-consuming cause we have to train each system three times with different random features. We will make revisions after obtaining the full results.
